Stage 3 · Language

One step at a time

How to order the steps, warn about the traps, and check that people are still with you.

Read these four lines from a demonstration.
  • The first thing you do is cut a hole in the metal.
  • Next, rub the plastic bottle with sandpaper.
  • When you’ve done that, put the bottle in the hole.
  • While the glue’s drying, fill the bottle with water.
Which one tells you to do two things at the same time?
Instructions and opinions fail for the same reason: the listener cannot see the structure.

This lesson covers two patterns of organisation rather than a verb form. The first is the language of sequenced instructions; the second is the fixed shape of an opinion paragraph. They look unrelated, but they solve the same problem: how to make somebody follow a line of thought they cannot see laid out in front of them.

When you talk somebody through a process, they cannot look ahead the way a reader of a manual can. Sequencers do that work for them: First of all… The next thing you do is… Once you’ve done that… Finally… Each phrase tells the listener where they are in the process. Alongside them sit the warning and checking phrases that prevent mistakes before they happen: Make sure you…, Be careful not to…

Instructions themselves are given in the imperative — the base verb with no subject. This is not rude in English when you are genuinely instructing: recipes, manuals and directions all use it. Softening it (you might want to…) is only necessary when you are telling an equal what to do in a situation where they did not ask.

The opinion paragraph has an equally fixed shape: a topic sentence that states the position, one or more reasons, an example or piece of evidence attached to each reason, and a conclusion that restates without repeating. The most common weakness in B1 writing is a reason with nothing behind it — which reads as the same opinion said twice — and a conclusion that smuggles in a brand-new argument.

Before you look at the table: the tables below give the sequencers and the paragraph markers in the order you use them. Read them as a sequence, not as a vocabulary list.
What to say, and when

Instructions use the plain verb. Cut a hole. Rub the bottle. Add the milk. No you, no to. The one exception is the opening: The first thing you do is cut…

The listener has a job too. A good demonstration is full of How do you do that?, What next? and Can you show me again? Somebody who says nothing has not understood.

The two that get confused. When you’ve done that means after it is finished. While the glue’s drying means during. Getting them the wrong way round ruins the instructions.

Warnings carry the obligation forms recycled: You have to measure carefully, You mustn’t cut it too big, You don’t have to use all the glue.

Full grammar reference — giving instructions in sequence, and building an opinion paragraph

What it is

Two connected pieces of functional language. The first is the sequencing set used when you talk somebody through a process: ordinal markers, warnings and checks. The second is the fixed shape of an opinion paragraph: a topic sentence, supporting reasons with examples, and a conclusion. Both are patterns of organisation rather than verb forms.

What it means, and what it does

Instructions and opinions both fail for the same reason: the listener or reader cannot see the structure. Sequencers tell somebody where they are in a process (first … once you’ve done that … finally), and paragraph markers tell a reader where they are in an argument (I believe … one reason is … for example … to sum up). In both cases the signposts are what make the content usable.

When and why we use it

This lesson covers two patterns of organisation rather than a verb form. The first is the language of sequenced instructions; the second is the fixed shape of an opinion paragraph. They look unrelated, but they solve the same problem: how to make somebody follow a line of thought they cannot see laid out in front of them.

When you talk somebody through a process, they cannot look ahead the way a reader of a manual can. Sequencers do that work for them: First of all… The next thing you do is… Once you’ve done that… Finally… Each phrase tells the listener where they are in the process. Alongside them sit the warning and checking phrases that prevent mistakes before they happen: Make sure you…, Be careful not to…

Instructions themselves are given in the imperative — the base verb with no subject. This is not rude in English when you are genuinely instructing: recipes, manuals and directions all use it. Softening it (you might want to…) is only necessary when you are telling an equal what to do in a situation where they did not ask.

The opinion paragraph has an equally fixed shape: a topic sentence that states the position, one or more reasons, an example or piece of evidence attached to each reason, and a conclusion that restates without repeating. The most common weakness in B1 writing is a reason with nothing behind it — which reads as the same opinion said twice — and a conclusion that smuggles in a brand-new argument.

Typical situations

You need the first strand for explaining any process at work or at home, giving directions, and demonstrating something. You need the second for any piece of argued writing, from a forum comment to the essay at the end of this course.

  • Starting a process — First / First of all / Start by + -ing.First of all, fill the bottle with water.
  • Moving to the next step — Then / Next / After that / The next thing you do is.The next thing you do is rub the bottle with sandpaper.
  • Warning and checking — Make sure you… / Be careful not to… / Don’t forget to…Make sure you measure it carefully.
  • Marking a completed step — Once you’ve done that… / When it’s cooked…Once you’ve done that, flip it over.
  • Finishing — Finally / Lastly / And that’s it.Finally, leave it to cool for ten minutes.
  • Stating an opinion in writing — the topic sentence that opens the paragraph.I believe that competitive sport belongs in schools.
  • Supporting it — reason, then evidence or example.One reason is that children learn to lose. For example,…
  • Concluding — a closing sentence that restates, not repeats.To sum up, the benefits clearly outweigh the risks.

How it differs from similar structures

Finally = the last step or point · At last = relief that something took a long time · In the end = the eventual outcome. Only finally belongs in a set of instructions.
To sum up (spoken and written, neutral) · In conclusion (written, formal essays) · Overall (weighing two sides). Match the one you choose to the genre.

How to build it

Sequencer + imperative: First, + base verb + object — First, crack the egg into the bowl.
Completed step: Once you’ve + past participle, + imperative
Warning: Make sure you + base verb  ·  Be careful not to + base verb
Opinion paragraph: topic sentence → One reason is that… → For example,… → In conclusion,…
Imperative — affirmativeCrack the egg. · Rub the bottle with sandpaper.
Imperative — negativeDon’t overcook it. · Never buy things on impulse.
Softened instructionYou want to… / What you do is… / Try to…
Sequencers, front positionFirst, · Then, · After that, · Finally, — comma after each.
Topic sentenceI believe that… / In my view,… / It seems to me that…
Support and exampleOne reason is that… · This is because… · For example,… · For instance,…
ConcessionAlthough some people argue that…, · It is true that…, but…
ConclusionTo sum up,… · In conclusion,… · Overall,…

Usage notes and exceptions

  • The imperative has no subject and uses the base verb. It is not rude in instructions — recipes, manuals and directions all use it. Softening it (you might want to…) is only needed when you are telling an equal what to do.
  • Then can appear without a comma inside a clause (and then you flip it), but a sentence-initial Then, takes one.
  • Once you’ve done that uses the present perfect for a step that must be complete before the next one starts. This is the same ‘no future after a time conjunction’ rule as Lesson 5.
  • In an opinion paragraph, each supporting reason should have evidence or an example attached. A reason with nothing behind it reads as a repeated opinion.
  • For example and for instance are interchangeable and both take a comma. Such as is different: it introduces a noun, not a clause — sports such as rugby, not such as, children learn to lose.
  • A conclusion should not introduce a new argument. If a new point appears in the last sentence, it belongs in the body of the paragraph.

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • First of all you must to fill the bottle. → First of all, fill the bottle.Instructions take the imperative, and must never takes to.
  • Make sure that you will measure it carefully. → Make sure you measure it carefully.No future form in this clause.
  • Once you have done that, you will flip it over. → Once you’ve done that, flip it over.Keep the imperative for the next step.
  • In conclusion, another reason is that it is cheaper. → In conclusion, the advantages are clear.A conclusion restates; it does not add a new reason.
  • For example, such as rugby and swimming. → For example, rugby and swimming.For example and such as do the same job — use one.
  • At the end, leave it to cool. → Finally, leave it to cool.Finally marks the last step; at the end refers to a place.

More examples in context

  • first stepStart by filling the bottle with water and adding ten millilitres of bleach.
  • next stepThen rub the outside with sandpaper until it is rough.
  • checkMake sure you don’t crack the bottle while you rub it.
  • completed stepOnce you’ve done that, put it on the roof where the sun hits it.
  • warningBe careful not to overcook the first side.
  • last stepFinally, leave it for two hours and check the water is clear.
  • topic sentenceI believe that schools should teach practical skills alongside exams.
  • reasonOne reason is that most jobs test what you can do, not what you can recite.
  • exampleFor example, a chef needs precise timing far more than a certificate.
  • conclusionTo sum up, practical subjects prepare students for work, and they should not be optional.

A tip for remembering it

Use the same three-part discipline for both jobs. For instructions: step → check → next step. For a paragraph: claim → reason → example, then close. If a listener has to ask ‘and then what?’, or a reader has to ask ‘why do you think that?’, a signpost is missing.

Before you practise — the key rules

  1. Instructions use the imperative: base verb, no subject, no to.
  2. Sequence with first, then, after that, once you’ve done that, finally — comma after each at the front of a sentence.
  3. Warn with Make sure you… and Be careful not to…, and use no future form after them.
  4. An opinion paragraph runs: topic sentence → reason → example → conclusion.
  5. Every reason needs evidence or an example attached to it.
  6. A conclusion restates the argument; it never introduces a new point.

Stage 5 · Main input

One paragraph, one opinion

Read it as a writer. You are going to write one like it.

Before you read: should schools teach practical repair skills?

Decide first. The model takes one side; you do not have to agree with it.

Everybody should learn to fix one thing

I believe that every school should teach at least one practical repair skill. One reason is money: a computerized appliance is often overpriced to fix, so people throw it away and buy another one. If you can deal with a small fault yourself, you save both the cost and the object. For example, my neighbour was about to replace a washing machine because of a blocked pipe that took me ten minutes to clear. Another reason is confidence. Students who fail every test on paper often turn out to be excellent with their hands, and one lesson where they succeed changes how they see themselves. Of course, not everybody will become an engineer. To sum up, though, a skill that costs one afternoon to learn and saves money for forty years is worth the timetable space.

What the model does, in five moves
  • States the opinion in line one. Nobody has to guess what you think.
  • One reason, then a second. Two is enough for a paragraph.
  • One concrete example. A real washing machine beats three more adjectives.
  • Admits the other side once, in half a sentence, and moves on.
  • Closes by repeating the opinion in different words. Then stops.
